e.etymology: A modern American name that puts a K on the -siah sound of Josiah and Messiah. The same letters can also be read as a spelling of Keziah, one of Job's daughters in the Bible.
From Greek helios, sun. Helios was the Titan sun god who drove a four-horse chariot across the sky each day; his name survives in English words such as heliocentric and helium.

assoc.t: Helios, the sun god of Greek myth

e.etymology: A recent American name with no established source. It reads as Naomi with a K, in line with K- names such as Kaori and Kalani.

From the surname Leigh, a spelling of Lee, from Old English leah, a wood or clearing, for someone who lived by one. It is often used as a middle name and as the second half of compounds like Everleigh.
A double-n spelling of Marilyn, a 20th-century blend of Mary and the ending -lyn. Marilyn spread in the 1920s with Broadway star Marilyn Miller, well before Marilyn Monroe.
From Yiddish Hirshel, a pet form of Hirsh, deer. Hirsh was the traditional everyday counterpart of the Hebrew name Naftali, whom Genesis likens to a deer.
namesakes: Hershel Greene (the veterinarian farmer on The Walking Dead)

assoc.t: Hershel Greene of The Walking Dead

e.etymology: A spelling of Kelsey, an English surname from villages in Lincolnshire or from the Old English personal name Ceolsige, ship victory. Kelsey became a girls' name in the US in the 1980s.

A Latin American name made famous by Dayanara Torres of Puerto Rico, Miss Universe 1993. It is usually explained as an elaboration of Dayana, the phonetic Spanish spelling of Diana, or a reshaping of Deyanira.
namesakes: Dayanara Torres (Puerto Rican Miss Universe 1993 and actress)

e.etymology: A phonetic American spelling of Dante, the medieval Italian short form of Durante, from Latin durans, enduring. The name honors the poet Dante Alighieri.

assoc.t: Dante Alighieri, poet of the Inferno (same sound)

e.etymology: A Spanish surname, Márquez, son of Marcos (Mark). As a US first name it rose in the 1990s beside Marquis and Marquise, which sound similar but come from the French noble title.

assoc.t: Gabriel García Márquez, Nobel-winning Colombian novelist

e.etymology: The French form of Alan, a Breton name carried to England by followers of William the Conqueror. Its root is disputed: a Celtic word for rock, or the Alans, a steppe people who settled in Gaul.
namesakes: Alain Delon (French film star of Le Samouraï)
Alain Prost (four-time Formula One world champion)

e.etymology: A spelling of Janiya or Janiyah, an American coinage of the 1990s that extends Jan- names such as Jane and Janae with the -iya sound of Aaliyah and Shania.
From Hebrew Tirtsah, delight or pleasantness. In the Bible Tirzah is one of the five daughters of Zelophehad who won the right to inherit, and a city praised for its beauty in the Song of Songs.

assoc.t: Tirzah, Judah Ben-Hur's sister in Ben-Hur

e.meaning: John Paul: God is gracious, and small or humble
e.etymology: The Spanish double name Juan Pablo written as one word. Juan is John, from Hebrew for God is gracious; Pablo is Paul, from Latin paulus, small. Many families use it in honor of Pope John Paul II.
namesakes: Juan Pablo Montoya (Colombian driver, two-time Indianapolis 500 winner)

e.etymology: The Polish, Czech and Brazilian spelling of Isabella, from Isabel, the medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
A modern American name that gives Ireland, the country, the -lyn ending, in the style of Brooklyn and Jocelyn.
A spelling of Jaylee, a 20th-century American coinage that joins Jay and Lee, in the same family as Kaylee and Jaylynn.
A respelling of Alize, from French alizé, the trade wind. Alize took off as an American girls' name in the 1990s.
A modern elaboration of Kaylie with the -ana ending, which can also be read as Kay plus Liana.
A respelling of Beckham, an English surname from a Norfolk village whose Old English name means the homestead of a man called Becca.

assoc.t: David Beckham, English soccer star (spelled Beckham)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yo'av, joining a short form of the divine name with av, father. In the Bible Joab is King David's nephew and the commander of his army.
An English surname from the medieval personal name Hawkin, a pet form of Hal (Henry) or of a byname meaning hawk, with the patronymic -s.

assoc.t: Hawkins, Indiana, the town in Stranger Things

e.etymology: A respelling of Raven, the English word for the large black bird, from Old English hraefn.
From Arabic Zaydan, built on zayd, increase or growth; the surname Zidane is the same name. In the US it also serves as a spelling of the modern name Zayden.
Built from Ana and the -lie ending, in the pattern of Annalee and Analia.
From Japanese gohan, cooked rice or a meal, used as the name of Son Gohan in Dragon Ball. Parents choose it for the character; it is not a traditional Japanese given name.

assoc.t: Gohan, Goku's son in Dragon Ball Z

e.note: In Japanese, gohan is the everyday word for cooked rice or a meal.

e.etymology: A surname spelling of Wolf, an old English and German given name and byname taken from the animal.
A respelling of Jelani, a name used mainly by African American families and usually explained as Swahili for mighty.
A respelling of Bellamy, a surname from Old French bel ami, fair friend, brought to England by the Normans.
A respelling of Alani, from Hawaiian 'alani, the orange tree and its fruit.
A respelling of Zaire, the former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and of the Congo River, from a Kikongo word for river.
